raw_case_text: A 40-year-old male presented with the complaint of intermittent high-grade fever since 4 days and diffuse chest pain for 3 hours. The pain was moderate in intensity and was radiating to the nape of neck. There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and smoking. There was no history of cough, burning micturition, diarrhea, and vomiting. On examination, the patient was afebrile, and blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg with a pulse rate of 100 bpm. Chest examination was normal. Patient was admitted for further workup. Blood investigations were sent and results were pending. ECG showed ST elevation in II, I, aVL, V5, V6 [Figure 1]. Diagnosis of acute inferolateral wall STEMI was made. Patient was taken to the Cath. lab for primary angioplasty within an hour of admission. To our surprise, angiography came out be normal. Results of blood investigation showed white blood cell count was 7,000/mm3, platelet count was 60,000/mm3 indicating thrombocytopenia, hemoglobin was 10 g/dL, and blood glucose was 120 mg/dL. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) were raised. Liver function tests revealed a Gamma Glutamine Transferase (GGT) of 90 IU/L, Serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) of 110 IU/L, serum glutamic pyruvate transaminase (SGPT) of 126 IU/L, and LDH of 356 IU/L. Renal function tests showed a blood urea of 56 mg/dL and a serum creatinine of 1.5 g/dL. Blood smear was positive for plasmodium falciparum. Cardiac troponin was 0.05 ng/dL. Thorough history and examination of the patient was done after the procedure. It was revealed that the patient had history of chest pain that increased on breathing and decreased on leaning forward with radiation of chest pain to the nape of the neck. Also, examination revealed faint pericardial rub and moderately enlarged spleen on abdominal examination. History and examination findings with ECG changes were suggestive of pericarditis. Moreover, on careful reading of ECG, it was noticed that ST segment elevations were concave upward and there was PR segment elevation in aVR and PR segment depression in other leads characteristic of acute pericarditis. Further, echocardiography was done and mild pericardial effusion was seen. There were no regional wall motion abnormalities and left ventricular ejection fraction was normal on echocardiography. Thereafter, pertaining to the clinical picture, it was assumed that the pericarditis was the result of involvement of heart due to severe falciparum malaria. The patient was treated with an Artemisinin combination therapy for 3 days. The patient was treated for pericarditis with ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours for a week and then twice a day for another week. Serial ECG was done and no dynamic changes were noticed. The patient's symptoms improved after a week. Repeat blood smear at the end of antimalarial therapy showed no evidence of malarial parasites. Patient was discharged. ECG remained same on discharge and returned to normal during follow-up after 15 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presenting with intermittent high-grade fever for four days and acute chest pain radiating to the neck for three hours.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed intermittent high-grade fever four days prior to presentation. Three hours before hospital arrival, he experienced sudden-onset diffuse chest pain of moderate intensity radiating to the nape of the neck. Further history revealed that the pain worsened with deep inspiration and decreased when leaning forward.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, or smoking.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for cough, dysuria, diarrhea, or vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: Afebrile on arrival, pulse rate 100 beats/min, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg. Cardiovascular: Faint pericardial friction rub auscultated along the left sternal border; heart sounds normal. Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. Abdomen: Moderately enlarged, palpable spleen on abdominal examination.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count 7,000/mm3, platelet count 60,000/mm3 (thrombocytopenia), hemoglobin 10 g/dL, blood glucose 120 mg/dL; elevated ESR and CRP. Liver function tests: GGT 90 IU/L, SGOT 110 IU/L, SGPT 126 IU/L, LDH 356 IU/L. Renal function: Blood urea 56 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.5 g/dL. Cardiac troponin: 0.05 ng/dL. Baseline 12-lead ECG: Concave upward ST-segment elevations in leads I, II, aVL, V5, V6, with PR-segment elevation in aVR and PR-segment depressions across other leads, indicative of acute pericarditis. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Mild pericardial effusion, no regional wall motion abnormalities, preserved left ventricular ejection fraction.
objective.advanced_workup: Coronary angiography: Normal coronary arteries without obstructive coronary disease or thrombotic occlusion, ruling out acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute pericarditis secondary to Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Blood smear examination confirmed the presence of Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites. Coronary angiography ruled out STEMI/coronary occlusion.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for malaria with oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for 3 days. Pericarditis was treated with oral ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours for one week, followed by 600 mg twice daily for a second week. Symptoms resolved within one week, repeat blood smear showed complete clearance of malarial parasites, and follow-up ECG at 15 days showed complete normalization.
